newsitem.title: USA: Clinton downplays fear stock drop would hurt U.S.
newsitem.headline: Clinton downplays fear stock drop would hurt U.S.

text.p: President Clinton Friday played down fears that a correction of the high-flying U.S. stock market would end up hurting the economy.
"I don't think we should overconclude that," he told a news conference at which he unveiled his economic team for his second term.
In arguing that a stock market drop would not inevitably lead to an economic tailspin, Clinton pointed to the economy's ability to weather the October 1987 crash on Wall Street.
"Over the long term, if we have the discipline -- all of us -- to ride out the inevitable changes in the markets, the markets have produced a very steady growth," he said.

Clinton said he was "very pleased" that many Americans have made a lot of money from investing in the stock market. "I'm proud of the vibrant markets we have," he said, adding, "My job is to keep the underlying fundamentals sound."

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan rattled global markets last Friday after he said the central bank needed to be wary when "irrational exuberance" infects asset prices because that could end up doing damage to the economy.
Clinton declined comment on Greenspan's remarks.
During the news conference, the president reiterated his opposition to a balanced budget amendment to the constitution, saying that it was neither good policy nor needed.
He stressed though that he does favor balancing the budget, just not through an amendement to the constitution that could end up unduly tying policymakers' hands.

Clinton left open the possibility that he would agree to Republican demands for a cut in the capital gains tax as part of the bargaining that will take place between Congress and the administration over how to balance the budget.
A capital gains tax cut would not be a "show-stopper" in negotiations over the budget, Clinton said.
"I have already said that I was not inherently opposed to any kind of capital gains tax cut," he added.
